verdicts.why: B's mark is a stacked Langstroth hive: an outer cover, a super and a brood box with an entrance slot. That comes straight from what Dale sells and builds, and it uses flat shapes that will hold up embroidered, cut in vinyl or burned into wood. It still reads as a hive at 32 and 16 px; the cover blurs a little at 16 px but the shape stays clear. A's mark is a generic blocky M in a square frame that says nothing about bees or the river, and at 16 px it shrinks to a smudge in a box. Both set the name correctly in a similar serif and add nothing invented, so the mark decides it.

A's mark is a stacked Langstroth hive (lid, box, and a brood box with an entrance slot). It comes straight from what this client builds and sells. Its few solid blocks keep the same shape at 32 and 16 px and hold up in one color and reversed, though the thin lid softens a little at 16 px. B's mark is a blocky M in a square frame, which says nothing about bees or hives. Its M looks like a vague blob or shirt and turns into mush at 16 px. Both use the same well-set serif wordmark with the name spelled correctly, so the mark decides it.

B's mark uses O and R, the partners' surname initials, so it matches the firm's name, and its R keeps a clear bowl and leg at 16 and 32 px, in one color and reversed. A's second letter is a squared block that reads as A or H, not R, so the monogram looks like 'OA' or 'OH' and doesn't connect to 'Okafor & Reyes'. B's lockup has its own flaw: the mark is undersized next to the wordmark. Both spell the name correctly and add no invented text.

Both sheets spell the name exactly and add nothing the client didn't give, and both marks stay solid at 16 and 32 px and work in one color and reversed. The deciding problem is B's second letter: the boxy block with a notch on top and a slot below reads as 'A' or 'H', not 'R', so the monogram looks like 'OA' and points to the wrong firm. A's R has a clear bowl and leg, so 'OR' reads correctly at every size, though both are fairly generic initial monograms that don't draw on the client's own subject.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing invented, and both use the same rounded sans in the lockup, so the choice comes down to the mark. B's otter head rising above a single waterline is one bold, simple idea that stays the same shape at 16 and 32 px and holds up cleanly in one color and reversed. A's floating otter, with its separate head, tail and wavy water, reads more like a bear in a boat, and at 16 px it breaks into fragments that would also be hard to print well on a one-color swim cap.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing. A's mark, a round head with ears at a single waterline, keeps the same solid shape at 32 and 16 px and works in one color and reversed. B's shapes break up at small sizes: the stray vertical oval and the wave turn to noise at 16 px. B's idea also reads as a bear sitting in a boat rather than an otter swimming, while A, though plain, is one clear and well-built idea: a small animal head at the waterline.

The two pages use almost the same layout. B has a real three-part color system: a rust 'Harvest Signal' accent against the navy ink, where A's accent is a navy barely different from its ink. B's voice and imagery rules are also more specific to this client: they cite the 2,100 members from the brief, Rice County fence rows and the Lyons counter, and they ban tractor sunsets and red-X satellite dishes. A, by contrast, invents a 'P' monogram and a mark.svg file that the client doesn't have, and its 'Cream on Blue' swatch shows cream on cream with a 15.4:1 label that doesn't match its own 11.26:1 table.

nocouncil: mark.svg file and standalone 'P' monogram logo variant not in the brief

verdicts.why: B makes up a logo asset the client doesn't have: a 'P' monogram and a mark.svg file, with sizing rules, when the brief says the client has only logo.svg. A sticks to the real wordmark. A also has a real accent color, the rust Harvest Signal (#a4441a), which gives buttons and highlights a clear role. B's 'accent' is a navy almost the same as its ink color, so the page has no distinct accent and looks like a generic telecom navy. A's voice examples also use more real details from the brief, like '2,100 members who own this network together.'

council: '2026' printed next to 'Brand Guide' (a date, not a claim; minor)
nocouncil: 'P' monogram mark and a separate mark.svg file (client has only logo.svg)

verdicts.why: The two pages share nearly the same layout and neither invents facts. A has a visible error: its 'Linen on Plum' swatch is drawn as linen on light rather than on plum, which contradicts its own label. B gets that swatch right and fits the client better: it uses Atkinson Hyperlegible with larger body sizes for older readers, and its imagery rules are specific enough to judge a photo against (Dayton porches in daylight, written permission before showing anyone's face, no beaches or meadows). B has small flaws of its own: Atkinson's slashed zeros look odd in the numbers, and its one-color logo note names Night Plum while the logo is shown in Hearthstone Plum.

The two guides use nearly the same layout and neither invents facts, so smaller choices decide it. A pairs Fraunces with Atkinson Hyperlegible at an 18 px body size and says why: older readers. It also shows the Linen on Plum swatch on plum, and its imagery rules are more specific (Dayton porches in daylight, written permission before showing faces, no hospital beds). B uses a generic Source Serif/Sans pairing with smaller body text, shows its on-accent swatch as linen on white, which is confusing, and adds a 'Made with Hildegard' footer. B does make better use of the brief's '38 caregivers' fact in its voice section.

The two pages use nearly the same layout, but B's voice section is more useful: it has three Say/Not pairs, including one that names the Thursday over-50 class and one that ties the hours to members' shifts, and its color and logo specs say how they apply to shirt blanks, signs and embroidery. A has visible sloppiness: the footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg' and includes a 'Made with Hildegard' credit, and its fonts (Barlow and Archivo) feel more generic. B has its own small faults: the 'daylight from the showroom windows' imagery idea appears twice, it adds a few building details the brief doesn't give, and it stamps a 2026 date the client never stated.

nocouncil: bay doors (building detail not in brief)

verdicts.why: The two pages share the same layout, so the content decides it. A's voice section fits this client better: it has three Say/Not pairs, including the Thursday over-50 class and 'Open 5 a.m. before the shift', and its imagery rules ('close enough to see the chalk on the hands', no before-and-after photos without permission) are specific enough to check a photo against. B's footer has a production glitch ('files: logo.svg, logo.svg') and a stray tool credit, and its imagery rules are thinner. Both pages put a wrong contrast ratio on the on-accent swatch (A says 15.4:1, B says 17.6:1). A also has a second mismatch: its accent swatch says 5.8:1 but its own table says 5.07:1.

council: 'the building's brick and steel' (the brief never mentions the building's materials)
'old showroom windows' as a light source (inferred from the dealership, not stated)
nocouncil: 'daylight from the bay doors' (bay doors not in the brief)

verdicts.why: Both screens get the brief's items, quantities, times and places right. A is the more finished product: it names Two Creeks Farm, shows both pickup options equally with the Wednesday-noon cutoff, and uses a real iOS tab bar, while B quietly makes Thursday at the farm the member's default and leaves its empty state as a sparse card floating in a blank screen. A loses ground because its off-week screen offers a 'Change pickup day' button when there is no pickup to change, but B's empty state also gives the member nothing to do beyond the July 11 date.

nocouncil: Bottom tab bar with 'Pickup' and 'Account' sections not mentioned in the brief
'Change pickup day' action offered during the off week, when there is no box
council: Thursday at the farm shown as the member's assigned pickup, with Saturday as the alternative

verdicts.why: Both use the brief's box contents, quantities, pickup times and Wednesday-noon deadline correctly. B names Two Creeks Farm, gives both pickup options equal weight, and looks more like a finished iOS product with its tab bar and centered empty state. 'Change pickup day' action on the off-week screen when there is no pickup

verdicts.why: Both use the brief's content correctly and keep Biscuit and the Full groom selected in the error state. A shows every time with AM/PM and lists the services as clear radio rows with prices, and its sticky footer sums up the booking next to a large Confirm button. B drops AM/PM, so times like 1:00 and 8:30 are ambiguous; its service pills look less like a choice of options, though its error does better by striking through the lost 10:00 slot instead of hiding the time behind a 'Taken' label.

B shows AM/PM on every time, while A's bare '8:30', '1:00' and '12:00' are ambiguous for an appointment. B's error state keeps all three days visible, with a sticky summary of what is still selected and what to do next ('Pick another time'). A's error banner pushes Thursday's times below the fold and cuts them off. B also reads more clearly at a glance, with labeled For, Service and Open-times sections and a proper confirm bar with a summary, although its 'Taken' slot drops the original time label, which A's struck-through '10:00 booked' keeps.

Both use the brief's four items, numbers and suppliers correctly, sort low items first and flag the right low cells. A makes ordering the obvious next step with a per-row Order button and a labelled 'Below reorder point 3 / On track 1' grouping, while B has only one bulk 'Order low items' button, though B's per-store cell highlighting is a little easier to scan. Both empty states name Upland and 'generator' and offer to clear the search or search all stores; A's copy also explains what clearing will show, which keeps Jean's place slightly better.

Both use the brief's SKUs, quantities, reorder points and suppliers correctly and flag the right low cells. B looks more like a finished product, with low and on-track groups and an Order button on each row, but it adds Orders and Suppliers pages, a supplier filter and an Order button on the item that isn't low, none of which the brief asked for. A keeps to the brief with one clear 'Order low items' action, and its empty state keeps the table headers, says 'Showing 0 of 4 items at Upland' and offers Clear search and Show all stores.

nocouncil: Order button on the Kwikset row, which is not below its reorder point

verdicts.why: Both spell the name exactly, add nothing, and hold up at 16 px, in one color and reversed, so the choice comes down to the idea and the craft, where both are weak. A's solid M stands for Maumee, is a heavy shape that will embroider and burn cleanly, and is set with a deliberate bold serif. B's nested bracket shape doesn't clearly stand for any letter of the name or for hives and frames, and it sits next to a default-looking bold sans. Neither mark uses bees, honeycomb or the river, so A wins only narrowly.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing, and both marks are heavy, solid shapes that hold up at 16 px, in one ink and reversed. A's nested-bracket mark reads as the letter 'E', which isn't in the name, and its lockup is set in a default-looking bold sans. B's 'M' at least comes from the name, holds as a clear M at 16 px, and is paired with a deliberate bold serif that fits a rural Ohio supply store. Neither mark draws on bees, hives or the river, so B wins only slightly, mostly on relevance and type craft.

A's mark is an 'AR' monogram, but the firm is Okafor & Reyes, so the mark spells initials the client never gave and reads like another firm's name. B's O-enclosing-R monogram matches the name, and its solid round silhouette fits the small circular profile picture and works in one color and reversed, though its inner R turns to mush at 16 px. Both set 'Certified Public Accountants' too small to survive on vinyl, and A's thin, techy face for that line clashes with its serif name, while B's lockup is more consistent.

A's mark is an O with an R cut into it, which matches the firm name Okafor & Reyes. It stays a solid, recognizable round shape at 16 and 32 px, fits the small profile circle well, and holds up in one ink and reversed. B's 'AR' monogram uses initials that don't stand for the firm name (it reads as Adaeze plus Reyes, or as a stray 'AR'). That gives the firm an identity it never asked for, and B's thin, technical-looking 'Certified Public Accountants' line would break up on vinyl or letterhead.

nocouncil: 'AR' monogram initials that don't match the firm name Okafor & Reyes

verdicts.why: A's mark reads as an otter face with a wave beneath it. It keeps the same solid silhouette at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one ink and reversed, so it suits caps, signage and the app icon. B's pointed ears make the head read as a cat, not an otter, and the stray vertical bars in the face look like random marks rather than a clear idea. A's main weakness is craft: its wordmark is set small with cramped leading, but that is easier to fix than B's concept.

B's mark reads as an otter face (round head, two eyes, a nose) rising above a water wave. It keeps that same shape at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one ink and reversed. A's mark looks more like a cat or a castle, and the vertical bars inside it are hard to read and turn to mush at 16 px, so the otter idea is lost. B's lockup has a weakness: the two-line wordmark is small and tightly leaded next to the mark. A's wordmark is bolder and better balanced, but that doesn't make up for a mark that doesn't read as an otter.

Neither page invents facts: B's fact bar uses only figures from the brief (2,100 members, $65 for 500 megabits, no contracts or data caps, the Lyons office), and its 'Connected by community' headline is a slogan, not a claim. B's page has stronger hierarchy and feels more like this co-op, with tighter voice Say/Avoid pairs and photo rules a person could check a photo against. A has real strengths, including logo clear-space and minimum-size rules, a full contrast table and clearer color roles, but its footer has a 'logo.svg, logo.svg' glitch and the page reads more like a template.

Both pages stick to the brief's facts, but B is a more complete system: it adds logo usage rules (clear space and minimum size), names a specific role for each color, and gives a full contrast table with pass levels. A's color roles are single words like 'ground' and 'muted'. B's warm Loess/Wheat palette, slab headlines and specific imagery do's and don'ts feel more like rural Kansas than A's cool, generic telecom gray-blue. B has small craft slips: the footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg' twice and carries a 'Made with Hildegard' credit.

council: Tagline 'Connected by community.' is not in the brief (a minor invented slogan, not a factual claim)

verdicts.why: The two pages share nearly the same layout and neither invents any facts, so polish decides it. A's header has a glitch: 'BRAND GUIDE' and 'BRAND SYSTEM' are stacked and crowd the title. A also has a capitalization slip ('For Older adults') and a stray 'Made with Hildegard' footer. B's header is clean, it brings in Dayton from the brief, and its sage accent sets the palette apart from a single plum, which makes the system feel more specific to this client.

Both stick to the brief's facts and share nearly the same structure, with clear hex roles, contrast checks, named type pairings and good Say/Not voice examples. B has visible craft faults: its header stacks a redundant 'BRAND GUIDE' and 'BRAND SYSTEM' label crowded against the wordmark, it capitalizes 'For Older adults' mid-sentence, and its footer reads 'Made with Hildegard'. A's clean header and its Garden Sage accent beside the violet give the client a more distinctive, usable palette than B's all-plum one.

Neither guide invents any facts, and their color and type systems are almost the same. A has layout faults at the bottom of the page: the Caption row of its type scale runs into the footer rule, and its last imagery bullet runs into the footer, which also shows the stray 'Made with Hildegard' credit. B's page is clean and well spaced, and its imagery rules about shop light, safe setup and no age stereotypes fit this client more closely. A's voice section is slightly richer, with three Say/Not pairs to B's two, but that doesn't make up for the overlaps.

B has visible layout faults at the bottom of the page: the Caption row of the type scale and the last imagery bullet both run into the footer rule and footer text. A's page is clean, with nothing cut off or overlapping. Both use only facts from the brief and have similar systems (hex values with roles, contrast tables, named type pairing and scale). B's voice examples are a little richer and its Signal Red tied to farm iron is a nice touch, but that doesn't make up for the collisions, the stray 'For College' capital and the footer that lists logo.svg three times.
